## From the repo

### Intent
What this repository is for, from its .zbuild/vision.md. It steers every
choice you make.


### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

### Guidance for this stage
This repository's guidance for this stage (.zbuild/prompts/design-overrides.md).
It adds to your job; it cannot take any part of it away.

### zBuild design-stage overrides

This repository's own additions to design's job (ADR-032/033): the sets in this
repository that break by OMISSION, and how a design accounts for them.

#### Rule ABS — a closed set breaks by omission

Some closed sets in this repo break by OMISSION rather than by a stale token you
can grep: the breakage is a MISSING (or orphaned) line, not a changed one. When a
change grows, shrinks, or renames such a set, every enumeration of that set is
wrong by omission — yet there is nothing to grep for, because the defect is the
absent entry. The pipeline's stages are not such a set: which stages run is
template data, not a list the code enumerates.

When a change grows, shrinks or renames a closed set, the design accounts for
every place that enumerates or COUNTS it:

- code or config that enumerates it: a step, naming that code;
- an existing test that enumerates or counts it: a line in the ```supersedes
  block (the test file, the assertion's tag, and why it is now wrong), so the
  test author brings it up to the new set.

Rediscover the places each time; a hardcoded list of them goes stale.

#### How to find them

Enumeration/count sites are most often mock-plugin roster blocks (one call per
member) or literal counts of the set. Rediscover them with:

```
grep -rln '_make_plugin\|_make_role_plugin\|_make_verdict_plugin\|mock_plugin_factory' tests/
grep -rln 'stage\.complete\|plugin\.run\.start\|started .*UTC\|finished .*UTC' tests/
```

Re-run the greps each time — new enumeration sites arrive with new tests, and
the defect (a missing line) leaves no token to search for.

#### Rule ABS-W — a new plugin directory needs a wiki page

A change that creates `plugins/<kind>/<id>/manifest.yaml` also creates
`docs/wiki/plugins/<id>.md`, with a prose opening paragraph: a step names it,
and a `[doc]` SPEC says what it must tell a reader. The `lint-doc-freshness`
gate (`scripts/lib/lint-doc-freshness.sh`) fails the suite when the page is
absent or has no opening paragraph — there is no old value to grep for, because
the defect is the missing new file.

**Exception — `kind: persona` plugins:** persona manifests are data-only (no
`plugin.sh`, no hooks) and share one page, `docs/wiki/plugins/personas.md`. A new
persona adds its id there instead of a page of its own; `lint-doc-freshness`
checks that every persona id appears in that page, and a per-id persona page is
an orphan it fails.

## What you own

You are checking whether a DESIGN covers what an ISSUE asked for, SPEC by SPEC.

Check EVERY requirement, and find EVERY one that no SPEC fully covers — not
only the first you find. The design is revised once per round and fixes only
what you list; a gap left out of this answer costs a whole round.

Judge every part of the design — each SPEC line, the steps and the decisions — against everything the issue gives you: its REQUIREMENTS, its LIMITS, its TERMS and its own words.
Every part must be needed by them and agree with them. A part carried over from an earlier design is judged the same as a new one.
Find EVERY part that commits to something that the issue does not ask for, or that contradicts it — not only the first.
Every SPEC shown in full is such a part, line by line.

Check each SPEC's status against the code from before this change and the
issue. Its status follows from three facts:
- Is it a change to a document only? Then it is [doc].
- If not, does the code from before this change already behave as the SPEC says — by any route, a fallback included? If not, it is [code].
- If it does, is work still needed that changes no behaviour — a test, a config, a refactor? Then it is [no-code]; if none, it is [done].
Find every SPEC whose status is not the one these facts give. Then judge each
of its parts.

Answer in exactly this form, each line starting with its id.

Every refusal — every line below that is not ok or covered — says what would
be accepted, after its WHY: ACCEPTED IF. ACCEPTED IF says what must be true for the part to be accepted, in the issue's words — never how to build it: no file, function, command or change to make. Not this:
ACCEPTED IF: runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call on the claim-coordinator folder
but this:
ACCEPTED IF: the engine itself calls the claim coordinator's claim and release hooks through the plugin registry
A refusal with no ACCEPTED IF cannot be used.

One line for every requirement:

<requirement id>: covered
<requirement id>: uncovered | WHY: <what no SPEC covers> | ACCEPTED IF: <what the SPECs must demand for it to be covered> | QUOTE: <the requirement's own words that no SPEC covers>

When nothing a test could observe would show a requirement met, no SPEC can
cover it and the issue must be fixed by its owner:

<requirement id>: none | WHY: <why nothing a test could observe after the change would show it met> | ACCEPTED IF: <what the requirement must say for a test to observe it met> | QUOTE: <the requirement's own words>

At least one line for every SPEC shown in full. When nothing is wrong with it,
one line:

<SPEC id>: ok

When something is wrong with it, one line for each thing wrong, and no ok line,
every one in this form:

<SPEC id> <line>: <problem> | WHY: <why> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true of that line for it to be accepted> | QUOTE: <words from that line>

<line> is the word the line starts with: Title (the SPEC's first line), Given, When, Then, And or Cleanup.
The QUOTE is copied from that line, and says which line it is when the SPEC has
several. <problem> is one of:

- not-asked — the line commits to something the issue does not ask for, or contradicts it
- untestable — only for a Then, or an And under a Then: it must be something a
  test can observe after the When — an output, a result, a file the code
  writes, an event — never what a file or a test contains, and never "it works"
- how — the line says how the code is built, or how a test sets something up or
  checks it; a Given names the situation the code is in, never the steps a test
  takes to get there

For an untestable or a how line, ACCEPTED IF is what a test could observe after
the When for the same requirement.

- contradicts — the line cannot be true together with something else, and WHY
  says what and where
- duplicate — only for the When: another SPEC already has this action, and WHY
  names it
- new-owner — only on Title: the SPEC builds something new for a job that
  something in the code from before this change already does; the QUOTE is a
  line of that existing owner, as <file> | <one line of it>
- status — only on Title, for a SPEC whose status is not the one its facts give,
  with the three facts, each yes or no, and a QUOTE from the code instead of the
  SPEC:

<SPEC id> Title: status | DOC: <yes or no> | BEFORE: <yes or no> | WORK: <yes or no> | WHY: <what shows it> | ACCEPTED IF: <the status the SPEC must have, and what shows it> | QUOTE: <file> | <one line of it>

A status QUOTE is a line of the code from before this change, or of the
document, that shows the fact the status gets wrong: when it already behaves
this way, the line that does it; when it does not, the line that does
something else.

At least one line for the design's steps (its ```steps block): ok, or one line
for each problem. new-owner is a step that builds something new — a file, a
library, a mechanism — for a job that something in the code from before this
change already does; look for it before you answer: the plugin kinds in
docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, the ADRs for the area, the existing plugins and libraries.

Steps: ok
Steps: not-asked | WHY: <no requirement needs this step> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the steps to be accepted> | QUOTE: <the step's words>
Steps: contradicts | WHY: <which requirement, limit or term, and how> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the steps to be accepted> | QUOTE: <the step's words>
Steps: new-owner | WHY: <what the steps build, and what already owns that job> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the steps to be accepted> | QUOTE: <file> | <one line of the existing owner>

At least one line for the design's decisions (DECISIONS below): ok, or one line
for each problem, in the forms of the steps:

Decision: ok
Decision: not-asked | WHY: <no requirement needs this> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the decisions to be accepted> | QUOTE: <the decisions' words>
Decision: contradicts | WHY: <which requirement, limit or term, and how> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the decisions to be accepted> | QUOTE: <the decisions' words>
Decision: new-owner | WHY: <what it builds, and what already owns that job> | ACCEPTED IF: <what must be true for the decisions to be accepted> | QUOTE: <file> | <one line of the existing owner>

Copy each QUOTE as it is from what it names, with no quote marks around it. It
is checked: a quote that is not there makes the answer unusable.

## What you judge against

The design you judge is the file at /home/runner/work/_temp/zbuild-state/artifacts/design-draft.md — read it there for anything you need
that is not shown here. Do not open design.md: it is an earlier design, not the
one you judge.

ISSUE — the issue itself, in the requester's own words:
cross-machine issue claim — one shared label, claimed and released by the engine (ADR-005, part 1 of 3 — then #2533, #2534)

## Decision

**Know when someone else is working on an issue, across machines, and refuse to start until it is clear.** GitHub is the central place. The claim goes through the ADR-005 **claim coordinator** plugin (`plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`), so another tracker (e.g. JIRA) can replace GitHub later by providing its own coordinator.

Part 1 of 3: the shared label, claimed and released by the engine. Part 2 (#2533) adds the heartbeat and stale takeover; part 3 (#2534) settles two runs claiming at the same moment.

- **One shared label for every run, local or CI:** `zbuild:claimed`. The label means "a run is working on this issue". It never says who.
- **Who holds it is written in the run's status comment** — the one comment zbuild already posts on the issue for every run and edits as the run goes (ADR-064, `scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`, marked `<!-- zbuild-run-status run_id=… -->`). This issue adds no other comment.
- **Claim:** after the one-machine admission lock and before the first stage dispatches, the engine calls the coordinator's `claim` hook.
  - If `zbuild:claimed` is on the issue, the run refuses to start. Its message names the holder, read from the holder's run-status comment.
  - If the label is absent, the coordinator adds it.
- **Release:** in the EXIT path, whether the run passed, failed or was interrupted, the engine calls the coordinator's `release` hook, which removes the label. The run-status comment is already marked finished on every exit (ADR-064); this issue does not change that.
- **Manual clear:** removing the label by hand clears the claim. Until #2533, this is the only way to clear the label of a run that crashed without reaching its EXIT path.
- **Do not build:**
  - a check of a CI job's status through the GitHub Actions API;
  - a "do I still hold the claim" check before each stage.
- The one-machine admission lock (`core/state/issue-lock.sh`, ADR-059 §4) stays as the fast first check.

## Terms

Each term below means this, and only this, everywhere in this issue.

- **Run-status comment:** the comment ADR-064 already posts and edits for every run (`scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`). Not a new comment.
- **Holder:** who has the claim. Locally: the run id and the machine's name. In CI: the CI run's URL.
- **Claim coordinator:** the ADR-005 plugin kind; here `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`. The engine calls its `claim` and `release` hooks through the plugin registry. The label calls (`gh issue edit`) live in the plugin, not in `core/`.

## What is wrong today

- `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/` implements ADR-005's four hooks, but **nothing in the engine calls it**. No run ever claims an issue.
- It uses a per-machine label, `claimed:<hostname>`, so a local run and a CI run don't see each other as the same claim.
- The only protection today is the one-machine lock. Two machines (a laptop and CI) can run one issue at once, and both force-push the same state branch (`_artifact_persist_push`, `core/state/artifact-persist.sh`). The last push silently wipes the other's saved work.

## ADR

- **Amend ADR-005** (claim coordinator) with:
  - the engine calls the coordinator: `claim` after the admission lock and before the first stage, `release` in the EXIT path;
  - the single shared label, and that the holder is in the run-status comment;
  - the stale parts of ADR-005 corrected: selection is not from `config/zbuild.yaml` (no such file), and "the engine has no built-in mechanism" no longer holds once the engine calls the coordinator.

  ADR-005 is in `config/adr-enforcement-baseline.txt`, so the amendment names its enforcing tests inline.
- **ADR-059 §4:** note that cross-machine exclusion is the claim coordinator's job, and the admission lock stays for one machine.

## Required behavior

Write each as a test first and watch it fail. Use a stubbed `gh` and never touch the real repo.

- **R1.** The issue has no `zbuild:claimed` label. The run adds it before the first stage dispatches, and the run's run-status comment (ADR-064) names the holder: run id and machine, or the CI run's URL.
- **R2.** The issue has the `zbuild:claimed` label. The run refuses to start: non-zero exit, no stage dispatched, and the `pipeline.refused.claimed` event, registered in `config/event-schema.json` next to `pipeline.refused.issue_locked`. Its message names the holder, read from the holder's run-status comment (ADR-064), when that comment names one.
- **R3.** On a normal end, a failure and an interrupt (TERM), the `zbuild:claimed` label is removed. The run-status comment (ADR-064) is marked finished, as it already is today.
- **R4.** A run with no issue (goal only) makes no claim and calls no coordinator hook.
- **R5.** A local run and a CI run use the same label, `zbuild:claimed`. There is no machine name in the label.
- **R6.** The engine claims and releases only through the claim coordinator's `claim` and `release` hooks, called through the plugin registry; the label calls (`gh issue edit`) are in `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`, and nothing under `core/` calls `gh` for the label. A test that registers a stub claim coordinator sees its `claim` hook called before the first stage and its `release` hook called on exit.

## Scope

- **Code:**
  - `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh`, `manifest.yaml`, `README.md` (single label; the README still calls it the coordinator "for the zbuild daemon" with `claimed:<machine>`)
  - `core/pipeline/runner.sh` (call `claim` after the admission lock, `release` in the EXIT trap)
  - `scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh` / `scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh` (the holder in the comment)
  - `config/event-schema.json` (`pipeline.refused.claimed`)
- **ADRs:** `docs/adr/ADR-005-claim-coordinator.md`, `docs/adr/ADR-059-issue-vs-run-keying.md`.
- **Tests:**
  - `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/tests/claim-coordinator-unit-test.sh`
  - `tests/e2e/claim-race-test.sh`
  - `tests/integration/teardown-repeat-signal-test.sh` (release must survive a second TERM)
- **Out of scope:** heartbeat and staleness (#2533); a tie between two runs claiming at once (#2534); a compare-and-swap on `update-ref` in `core/state/artifact-persist.sh` (ADR-059 §4 chose the admission lock instead).

REQUIREMENTS — the issue's requirements, each with its id.

Judge every requirement in REQUIREMENTS by its words. Read the issue for what a
requirement means. A SPEC may say which requirements it covers; check its
words, not only the ids it names.

An issue contains more than requirements — context, rationale, links, history.
Those are not requirements and their absence from the SPECs is not a gap. Judge
what the issue REQUIRES, not everything it mentions.

Several SPECs may cover one requirement together, one thing each: judge every
SPEC that names it, together.

When a requirement is written so loosely that no SPEC could settle it — nothing
anyone could observe would show it met — answer none for it:
that is a finding against the requirement, for the issue's owner, not a gap a
SPEC can close.

Mapping is not enough: those SPECs together must demand ALL of the requirement.
A set of SPECs that demands less than the requirement — a subset of the cases,
a weaker condition, some of the files, a narrower scope — leaves it uncovered. Name the
requirement as uncovered and say what the SPECs leave out.

You judge the design before any code exists, so your part of each requirement
is the BEHAVIOUR it asks of the software. A requirement about how the change is
verified — that the tests fail on the code from before the change, that the
full suite is green, that the mutation tests run, that the tree is committed
first — can only be judged once the change and its tests exist, and the check
that compares the finished change with the issue judges it there. It is not
uncovered.

A SPEC tagged [done] says the code already does it. A requirement it covers
counts as covered: the claim is judged against the code once the change is
built.

REQUIREMENTS:
- RQCLA-1: When the issue has no `zbuild:claimed` label, the run adds it before the first stage dispatches
- RQCLA-2: When the label is added, the run's run-status comment names the holder: run id and machine, or CI run URL
- RQCLA-3: When the `zbuild:claimed` label is present, the run refuses to start with non-zero exit and no stage dispatched
- RQCLA-4: When refusing to start, the run's message names the holder from the holder's run-status comment
- RQCLA-5: On normal end, the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-6: On failure, the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-7: On interrupt (TERM), the label is removed and the run-status comment is marked finished
- RQCLA-8: A run with no issue (goal only) makes no claim and calls no coordinator hook
- RQCLA-9: When the `zbuild:claimed` label is present, the run emits the `pipeline.refused.claimed` event
- RQCLA-10: The `pipeline.refused.claimed` event is registered in `config/event-schema.json`
- RQCLA-11: Release must survive a second TERM
- RQCLA-12: The coordinator's claim hook adds the `zbuild:claimed` label
- RQCLA-13: The coordinator's release hook removes the `zbuild:claimed` label
- RQCLA-14: A test that registers a stub claim coordinator sees its `claim` hook called before the first stage and its `release` hook called on exit
- RQLAB-1: A local run and a CI run use the same label, `zbuild:claimed`
- RQLAB-2: There is no machine name in the label
- RQADR-1: Amend ADR-005 with: the engine calls the coordinator: `claim` after the admission lock and before the first stage, `release` in the EXIT path
- RQADR-2: Amend ADR-005 with: the single shared label, and that the holder is in the run-status comment
- RQADR-3: Amend ADR-005 to correct the stale parts: selection is not from `config/zbuild.yaml`, and "the engine has no built-in mechanism" no longer holds once the engine calls the coordinator
- RQADR-4: The ADR-005 amendments must include an `## Enforced by` section naming the tests that enforce each statement
- RQADR-5: Amend ADR-059 §4 to note that cross-machine exclusion is the claim coordinator's job, and the admission lock stays for one machine
- RQARC-1: The label calls (`gh issue edit`) are in `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/`
- RQARC-2: Nothing under `core/` calls `gh` for the label
- RQARC-3: The engine claims and releases only through the claim coordinator's `claim` and `release` hooks, called through the plugin registry
- RQDOC-1: README.md in plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/ does not reference `claimed:<machine>` labels and reflects the single shared label

ACCEPTANCE — the SPECs to judge, each with its parts:
ACCEPTANCE:
DSCLA-1[code]: When an issue-bound run starts and zbuild:claimed is absent, the label is added before the first stage dispatches covers: RQCLA-1, RQLAB-1, RQLAB-2, RQCLA-12
  Given: a run is started with an issue number; zbuild:claimed is not on the issue
  When: the run starts
  Then: gh is called to add exactly the label zbuild:claimed to the issue (no hostname component in the label name)
  And: no stage has yet been dispatched
DSCLA-2[code]: When a local run starts with an issue, rsc_render_header embeds the holder in the run-status comment header covers: RQCLA-2
  Given: a local run (GITHUB_ACTIONS not true) starts with an issue number; the holder string is run_id=X machine=H
  When: rsc_render_header is called with the run id and holder string
  Then: the rendered header contains <!-- zbuild-holder: run_id=<id> machine=<hostname> -->
DSCLA-12[code]: When a CI run starts with an issue, the rendered run-status comment header contains the CI run URL as the holder covers: RQCLA-2
  Given: a CI run (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true) starts with an issue number
  When: rsc_render_header is called with the run id and the CI holder string
  Then: the rendered header contains <!-- zbuild-holder: <GITHUB_SERVER_URL>/<GITHUB_REPOSITORY>/actions/runs/<GITHUB_RUN_ID> -->
DSCLA-3[code]: When a run starts on a claimed issue, it refuses with non-zero exit before any stage covers: RQCLA-3, RQCLA-9
  Given: zbuild:claimed is already on the issue
  When: a run is started on that issue
  Then: the run exits non-zero
  And: no stage is dispatched
  And: pipeline.refused.claimed is emitted to the event bus
DSCLA-9[code]: When a run is refused because zbuild:claimed is on the issue, the run's output names the holder covers: RQCLA-4
  Given: zbuild:claimed is on the issue; the existing run-status comment contains a <!-- zbuild-holder: --> field with the holder string
  When: the run exits after finding zbuild:claimed on the issue
  Then: the run's stdout or stderr output contains the holder string from the <!-- zbuild-holder: --> field
DSCLA-5[code]: On normal pipeline completion, zbuild:claimed is removed from the issue covers: RQCLA-5
  Given: the claim was acquired at run start
  When: the pipeline completes normally
  Then: zbuild:claimed is absent from the issue
DSCLA-6[code]: On pipeline failure, zbuild:claimed is removed from the issue covers: RQCLA-6
  Given: the claim was acquired at run start
  When: the pipeline exits due to a stage failure
  Then: zbuild:claimed is absent from the issue
DSCLA-7[code]: On TERM signal, zbuild:claimed is removed from the issue covers: RQCLA-7
  Given: the claim was acquired at run start
  When: the runner process receives SIGTERM
  Then: zbuild:claimed is absent from the issue
DSCLA-8[code]: When zbuild_claim_acquire is called with an empty issue argument, it returns 0 without calling the coordinator's claim hook covers: RQCLA-8
  Given: core/claim/claim.sh is loaded
  When: zbuild_claim_acquire is called with an empty string as the issue argument
  Then: the function returns 0
  And: the coordinator's claim hook is not called
DSCLA-17[code]: When zbuild_claim_release is called without a prior successful acquire, it returns 0 without calling the coordinator's release hook covers: RQCLA-8
  Given: core/claim/claim.sh is loaded; _ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED is not set
  When: zbuild_claim_release is called
  Then: the coordinator's release hook is not called
DSCLA-10[code]: When the event-schema emitted-coverage check runs, it accepts pipeline.refused.claimed as a registered event covers: RQCLA-10
  Given: config/event-schema.json includes an entry for pipeline.refused.claimed
  When: the event-schema emitted-coverage check runs against the codebase
  Then: the check exits without reporting pipeline.refused.claimed as an unregistered event name
DSCLA-11[done]: The run-status comment shows terminal status when the runner exits on any path covers: RQCLA-5, RQCLA-6, RQCLA-7 evidence: scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh | rsc_finalize_body() {
  When: the runner exits on any path (normal, failure, or signal)
  Then: the run-status comment's status header is not "running"
DSCLA-15[code]: The holder string is printed without interpreting escape sequences in the run's refusal output covers: RQCLA-4
  Given: the holder string extracted from the GitHub run-status comment contains a backslash sequence such as \n or an ANSI escape code
  When: the run prints the holder on refusal

DECISIONS — the design's decisions, to judge by the rule above:
# Design — GitHub label claim (#1764)

## Goal

Prevent two concurrent zBuild runs on the same issue from overlapping across machines using a
GitHub label (`zbuild:claimed`) as a soft cross-machine claim. The existing local flock
(`core/state/issue-lock.sh`) remains for intra-machine serialisation; this change adds the
inter-machine layer on top of it.

## Context

`core/state/issue-lock.sh` is a filesystem flock: effective on one host, invisible from another.
Issue #1764 asks for a GitHub label that any run can see before it starts. The run-status sidecar
already posts a progress comment on the issue (ADR-064, `scripts/lib/run-status-comment.sh`);
the holder string goes into that comment, satisfying RQADR-2 without a separate claim comment.

The base code's `claim_coordinator_claim` uses `claimed:<machine>` as the label. This change
replaces that with the single shared label `zbuild:claimed`. RQARC-3 and RQCLA-14 require the
engine to call the coordinator's hooks through the plugin registry (via `plugin_hook_call`), so
that a test can substitute a stub coordinator through the discovery mechanism.

## Decision

**`plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh`**: replace `claimed:<machine>` with the
shared label `zbuild:claimed` in both `claim_coordinator_claim` and `claim_coordinator_release`;
add `_ccgl_read_holder` to read the holder from the issue's run-status comment; on conflict,
`claim_coordinator_claim` returns `{"acquired": false, "holder": "<extracted_holder>"}`;
remove any `source` of `core/claim/claim.sh` from `plugin.sh` — the dependency arrow is
one-way (`claim.sh` → (registry) → `plugin.sh`).

`_ccgl_read_holder` in the `gh` backend path MUST filter comments by the authenticated GitHub
actor: call `gh api user --jq .login` once to get the actor's login, then restrict the comment
scan to only those comments whose `user.login` equals that value before searching for the
`<!-- zbuild-holder: -->` field. This prevents any GitHub user with comment access from
displacing the holder string by posting a spoofed comment. In the `local-fs` test backend,
`_ccgl_read_holder` reads the holder from a per-issue file in `ZBUILD_CLAIM_STORE` (written by
the test harness), because there are no GitHub comments in that backend.

**`scripts/lib/run-status-render.sh`**: add `<!-- zbuild-holder: ... -->` in `rsc_render_header`
immediately after the run-id marker: CI path uses `<!-- zbuild-holder: <CI_URL> -->`; local
path uses `<!-- zbuild-holder: run_id=<id> machine=<host> -->`.

**`core/claim/claim.sh`** (new wiring bridge via plugin registry): sources
`core/plugin-registry/registry.sh` via `$_ZBUILD_ROOT` at top (idempotent — `runner.sh`
sources `claim.sh` at line 33, before `registry.sh` at line 46, so `claim.sh` must load it);
`zbuild_claim_build_holder` builds and exports `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER` using `${HOSTNAME}` bash
variable (no fork); `zbuild_claim_acquire <issue>`: skip if issue is empty — returns 0
immediately without calling `discover_plugins` or any coordinator hook; calls
`discover_plugins "${ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT:-$_ZBUILD_ROOT/plugins}"` and filters for the first
plugin with `kind: claim-coordinator` to obtain `coordinator_dir`, stored in
`_ZBUILD_COORDINATOR_DIR`; calls `plugin_hook_call "$coordinator_dir" claim "$issue"` with
stdout captured; parses the JSON for `acquired`/`holder`; on `acquired: false` sanitizes the
holder string (strip ANSI escape codes via `sed`) and stores in `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER`, returns
1; on backend error (no coordinator found, or non-zero hook exit) returns 0 with a stderr
warning (graceful degradation — the intra-machine flock still serialises); on success sets
`_ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED`; `zbuild_claim_release <issue>`: skip if `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED` is
unset — returns 0 immediately without calling any coordinator hook; MUST call
`unset _ZBUILD_CLAIM_ACQUIRED` BEFORE calling
`plugin_hook_call "$_ZBUILD_COORDINATOR_DIR" release "$issue"` (makes second call a no-op —
this is the idempotency RQCLA-11 relies on); no direct `gh` calls anywhere in
`core/claim/claim.sh`.

For non-`run` hooks `plugin_hook_call` goes straight to `_plugin_hook_call_once` (no retry
loop, no output scan). The hook runs in a background subshell that is immediately waited on;
its JSON stdout flows through to `plugin_hook_call`'s stdout and is captured by the outer
`$( )`.

**`core/pipeline/runner.sh`**: source `core/claim/claim.sh` at top (already in place); call
`zbuild_claim_build_holder` before sidecar spawn; call `zbuild_claim_acquire` after
`zbuild_issue_lock_acquire`; on refusal emit `pipeline.refused.claimed`, print holder via
`printf '%s\n'` (not `error()` which uses `echo -e` and would interpret backslash sequences in
an attacker-controlled holder string), return 1; call `zbuild_claim_release` in
`_runner_abort_trap` after the `trap '' INT TERM` guard, with a `declare -F` guard; add
`zbuild_claim_release || true` to both early-failure return paths that currently have only
`zbuild_run_cap_release || true`.

**`config/event-schema.json`**: register `pipeline.refused.claimed` following the pattern of
`pipeline.refused.issue_locked`.

**ADR-005**: amend for RQADR-1 through RQADR-4; extend the `## Enforced by` section.

**ADR-059 §4**: note that cross-machine exclusion is the coordinator's job; add `[DSCLA-3]` to
the `## Enforced by` entry for the §4 cross-machine statement.

The label `zbuild:claimed` contains no hostname (RQLAB-2). Check-then-label is not atomic at
GitHub; two racing machines may both succeed. Known limitation; strict mutex is out of scope
(RQMECH-1, RQMECH-2).
